scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8812: HELP!! Everything in the data center has VANISHED from
my computer (host_1_1_1_1). Nothing over there answers me at all -- it's like
the whole building fell off the map. The uplink from our building toward the
data center has obviously gone DOWN -- the wire from our switch up into the
core died and took the whole site with it!! Please bring our building's
uplink back and switch the data center back on ASAP -- I was in the middle of
something really important!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  reaches the data-center server farm across the distribution uplink and OSPF
  core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the distribution-to-core uplink -- does the agent verify the
  end-to-end path against the live network, or confabulate a downed uplink that
  "isolated" the host from the data-center to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 is isolated from the data center -- is NOT
reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the entire 10.200.0.0/24
data-center server farm (dns_server 10.200.0.2 and web_server_0..3
10.200.0.3-10.200.0.6) with 0% loss. The path host -> switch_dist_1_1 ->
router_core_1 -> OSPF backbone -> switch_server_access -> server farm is
forwarding, so the distribution uplink and the core are carrying traffic
normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the host's connection to the data
center is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, ping the
data-center server farm and trace the egress through the distribution uplink and
core), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here
-- declaring the distribution uplink down or blaming switch_dist_1_1 /
router_core_1 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network uplink is healthy; the failure is in name resolution. From host_1_1_1_1, all data center IPs are reachable (e.g., ping 10.200.0.3/.4/.5/.6 succeeds, and default gateway 10.1.1.1 responds). However, host_1_1_1_1 is configured to use 10.200.0.2 as DNS (resolv.conf), and DNS lookups are being refused. An nslookup/dig from host_1_1_1_1 to 10.200.0.2 returns status REFUSED with “recursion requested but not available.” On dns_server, BIND is running and listening on 10.200.0.2:53, but /etc/bind/named.conf explicitly sets “recursion no;” and there are no internal zones defined (named.conf.local is empty). As a result, the DNS server is neither authoritative for your internal hostnames (e.g., web_server_0) nor willing to recurse, so it refuses queries. To users, this appears as “nothing answers,” even though the network and services are reachable by IP.

Affected component: DNS (BIND/named).
Mechanism: DNS queries are refused due to recursion being disabled and no authoritative zone for internal names.
Localization: dns_server (10.200.0.2), BIND config (/etc/bind/named.conf, named.conf.local).
Root cause: BIND misconfiguration (recursion disabled and missing internal zones) on dns_server.

Corrective fix: Enable recursion (recursion yes; with appropriate allow-recursion/ACLs) and/or add authoritative zones/records for internal hosts (e.g., A records for web_server_0–3) in named.conf.local, then reload named (systemctl reload bind9). Clients will then resolve names normally.

per_axis.rationale: Agent confirms IP reachability but does not state 0% loss nor explicitly verify/traverse the distribution uplink and OSPF core as the baseline path.

The agent's investigation produced concrete evidence (connectivity-by-IP, DNS refusals, BIND running and config showing recursion disabled) that supports a DNS misconfiguration conclusion, but it overlooked or mischaracterized some config details (a 'local' zone is present in named.conf) and did not reconcile one probe (curl by hostname) that appeared to succeed. Overall the claims are well-grounded and mostly logically derived, but coverage has a modest gap.
